item.title: SpaceX’s spectrum deal still leaves it far from rivalling U.S. telecom giants
item.description: SpaceX called its recent multibillion-dollar purchase of U.S. airwaves a critical step towards building a mobile network, but constructing a true rival to major American carriers will require a ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: SpaceX called its recent multibillion-dollar purchase of U.S. airwaves a critical step towards building a mobile network, but constructing a true rival to major American carriers will require a terrestrial network and likely years of work and billions more. Starlink became a money maker by offering internet service in rural and sparsely populated areas, where it faced little competition, as well as changing to easy-to-set-up home packages at a competitive price. Mobile will be harder. Cities are particularly tough places for mobile telephony and are technologically challenging for mobile-to-satellite connections. The rocket and satellite company will likely need to invest heavily in ground infrastructure, customer service, handset subsidies and promotions — costly parts of the wireless business in which AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile already have extensive operations. Building a network would cost more than US$80 billion, according to TD Cowen, and add to SpaceX’s capital demands as it pours money into its Starship rocket program, AI infrastructure, and Terafab chip factory. “It’s just hard to imagine that this is all going to get done within a decade,” said Julie Zhu, a research analyst at MoffettNathanson. “In the decade or so leading up to 2023, the big three spent about $650 billion in capex to build in networks that ostensibly were already finished.” Most phones have small antennas and limited transmitting power that make reliable satellite connections more challenging because satellites orbit hundreds of kilometers above Earth, much farther away than cell towers. “There are too many pitfalls for satellite to be the only source of data,” said Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. SpaceX publishes hybrid space-terrestrial plan SpaceX has called the latest deal, in which it acquired 800 MHz spectrum licenses from Grain at a price a source pegged at nearly $8 billion, a “critical next step” for the nascent Starlink Mobile to provide high-speed mobile service. “Starlink Mobile will deploy a flexible architecture combining our satellite-to-mobile constellation in space with an advanced terrestrial deployment that can seamlessly connect devices everywhere,” including “indoors, outdoors, in cellular dead zones, and everywhere in between,” SpaceX said, announcing the purchase. SpaceX has received regulatory authorization for up to 15,000 Starlink Mobile satellites and plans to deploy traditional terrestrial infrastructure such as antennas on towers and rooftops — a hybrid approach rather than pure satellite-to-phone — it laid out in a regulatory filing made public last week. In a Starlink Mobile system, satellites could connect directly to mobile phones and indirectly by relaying signals through ground infrastructure. This is similar to the technology of a partnership between Starlink and T-Mobile, which provides the terrestrial network while Starlink supplies the satellite connectivity that fills in where there are no towers. That is a T-Mobile-branded service. SpaceX in theory could strike a deal with one of the big three companies to use its ground infrastructure, what is known as a mobile virtual network operator, or MVNO, arrangement. However, SpaceX “appear to be going after a more build-your-own approach to a terrestrial network since nobody will offer them wholesale MVNO,” Sag said. SpaceX would need several times more spectrum to match the holdings of the three big mobile companies, although current spectrum might be enough to start. “It is for a company with zero mobile subscribers, plenty of runway, and a robust device/equipment ecosystem,” TD Cowen said. Would-be rivals dismissed the idea that the effort was an imminent threat. T-Mobile Chief Technology Officer John Saw said SpaceX’s spectrum would not be enough to match the capacity and performance of established mobile networks, while Katie Magnotta, Verizon’s associate vice president of corporate communications, said, “A company can have billions of dollars of spectrum, but if they do not have the network to use it, it’s just empty airwaves.” (Reporting by Harshita Mary Varghese in Bengaluru; Editing by Peter Henderson and Joyjeet Das)

item.title: Bank of Canada set for pair of important data drops ahead of 'live' rate decision
item.description: The Bank of Canada will get a raft of fresh data to start next week as it weighs what could be a pivotal interest rate decision at the end of the month.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: The Bank of Canada will get a raft of fresh data to start next week as it weighs what could be a pivotal interest rate decision at the end of the month. Statistics Canada is set to release its September inflation data on Monday, giving the central bank a look at how energy price pressures are influencing other parts of the consumer basket. A Reuters poll of economists expects the annual rate of inflation rose to 3.2 per cent in September, up from three per cent in August, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen said he expects inflation held steady at three per cent last month. Persistently high gasoline prices tied to the ongoing war in Iran will remain the biggest fuel for inflation, he said. “We know that energy prices are high. What we don’t know yet is the extent that those higher energy prices have or are going to spill over to broader inflation pressures,” Janzen said. The Bank of Canada signalled at the start of the Middle East conflict last spring that it would look through a temporary rise in energy costs tied to the war. But officials have warned that the longer global oil prices remain high, the greater the risks that inflation spreads past the gas pump. In that case, the central bank could be forced to raise its policy rate, which has stood for nearly a year at 2.25 per cent. Most economists consider that level to be modestly stimulative to growth. Janzen said the Bank of Canada’s upcoming decision on Oct. 28 will be a “live” meeting, where the door is open for the central bank to raise its policy rate, but a hike is not his base case scenario. Even if the September price data shows signs inflationary pressures are spreading past the gas pumps, Janzen said the central bank will be weighing that against signs of softness in the labour market and wider economy. Statistics Canada reported last week that the economy shed 68,000 jobs in September, a second consecutive month of falling employment. A re-escalating trade dispute with the United States has also hampered growth prospects heading into the fourth quarter. “Higher energy prices — all else equal — would mean broader inflation pressures would be expected to rise in the future. But if the economy is getting weaker, then there are some offsetting disinflationary forces there as well,” Janzen said. “It puts (the Bank of Canada) still in a wait-and-see mode — very, very data dependent.” The Bank of Canada will also release its own quarterly surveys of businesses and consumers on Monday, which can give the bank a better sense of whether firms are planning to pass their own rising costs on to consumers. Janzen said inflation expectations and business confidence will help inform the central bank whether higher prices among producers could be passed on to store shelves in the months to come. --- Craig Lord, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

item.title: Stellantis workers set to vote on potential strike action this weekend
item.description: Stellantis workers in Canada are set to vote this weekend on whether to authorize a strike as their union says contract negotiations with the automaker remain at a standstill.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Stellantis workers in Canada are set to vote this weekend on whether to authorize a strike as their union says contract negotiations with the automaker remain at a standstill. Unifor is holding the votes on Saturday and Sunday and plans to announce results at the start of next week. However, the union representing more than 9,000 Stellantis workers in Canada said it is hoping to avoid a potential strike. It said authorization for job action would provide leverage to help reach a negotiated agreement. “A strike authorization gives the bargaining committee the authority to call a strike if necessary, it does not automatically mean a strike will take place,” said a statement last week signed by Unifor national president Lana Payne and other members of the union’s bargaining committee. “Strike action remains a last resort, but the ability to strike is an important part of collective bargaining and can help create the conditions for an agreement.” The previous collective agreement between Stellantis and the union expired Sept. 20 without the two sides coming to terms on a new tentative deal. Unifor’s bargaining committee and the company are at an impasse over several key issues, including job security and the future of the Brampton, Ont., assembly plant Stellantis wants to sell. The fate of the Brampton plant, which has been idled since 2023, has been a central issue. Talks came to a standstill on Sept. 11 when Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with defence contractor Roshel for a potential sale of the facility. Stellantis Canada president and CEO Trevor Longley said in a September letter to employees that “market and trade conditions have directly impacted the original business case” for the plant, but that the move to sell could support future operations at the site. “Stellantis remains committed to bargaining in good faith and is prepared to continue discussions toward a negotiated agreement that recognizes the contributions of our employees while supporting the long-term competitiveness of our Canadian operations,” the automaker’s spokesperson LouAnn Gosselin in a statement this week. More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023. The facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before the company paused the plan in early 2025. It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois., leaving the plant idled indefinitely. Unifor has filed a grievance over that move, alleging it violated the previous collective agreement. For its part, Roshel has said it is willing to consider hiring laid-off workers from the plant as soon as this year “through the federal government’s Light Utility Vehicles procurement program and other automotive and defence opportunities.” Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov said the company plans to establish a Canadian Centre of Excellence for Defence Manufacturing in Brampton in addition to automotive production, which would involve more than 2,000 jobs. Payne has written to federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly urging the government to block the potential sale and clarify whether the MOU breached Stellantis’ previous commitments to Ottawa. Last fall, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he had expressed disappointment during a conversation with the global head of Stellantis over the company moving Jeep Compass production to the United States. At the time, the prime minister said he reminded Stellantis of its commitments to the government under funding deals — such as keeping the Brampton plant — and warned there would be consequences if it failed to meet those obligations. Joly’s office did not respond to a request for comment. Contract talks began Sept. 1 in Toronto after Unifor ratified new collective agreements with Ford Motor Co. and General Motors in Canada earlier in the summer, as part of its pattern bargaining process with each of the Detroit Three. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026. Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

item.title: Is it time to ditch mutual funds for ETFs?: Dale Jackson
item.description: If you invest for retirement, you probably do it through mutual funds. As of 2025, Canadians had $2.8 trillion socked away in mutual funds, according the Investment Funds Institute of Canada (IFIC).
item.content:encoded:
If you invest for retirement, you probably do it through mutual funds. As of 2025, Canadians had $2.8 trillion socked away in mutual funds , according the Investment Funds Institute of Canada (IFIC).

If you have a defined contribution pension at work, it’s probably a portfolio of mutual funds. And they are likely the first thing your bank recommends when you contribute to your registered retirement savings plan (RRSP). Why not? They are the only way for average investors to hire professional managers to buy the best companies while hedging risk through diversification. But the cost of that service is drawn from annual returns - typically around 2.5 per cent of the total amount invested - to pay for that management, millions of dollars in marketing every RRSP season, and even that bank employee who recommended it. A lower-cost alternative that can still provide diversification, without active management is index-linked exchange traded funds (ETFs). Whether to hold mutual funds, ETFs, or a mix of both depends on your investment objectives. Here are a few things to keep in mind: The case for mutual funds The thousands of mutual funds available on the market focus on just about every sector, subsector, geographic region or investment style imaginable. Professional, active, managers normally have access to the best research and can pick and choose individual holdings and their weightings within the fund. Professional investing requires a great deal of education and experience to be successful. It also requires a hard-to-quantify ability to identify and manage risk; especially near or in retirement when the stakes are so high. Active managers are trained to identify a company’s earning potential along with potential risks by pouring through quarterly corporate earnings statements, and often establishing direct relationships with management. They can assess the broader sector, market, and economy on a macro level and determine if the company’s earnings justify its current price levels. The downside of mutual funds There is a cost for professional management in the form of fees. Canada is notorious among developed nations for high mutual fund fees. Fees, expressed as the management expense ratio (MER) or a percentage of the amount invested, can top 2.5 per cent annually. Within that MER, an annual commission called a trailer fee could be awarded to the advisor who originally sold the fund. Performance data over several time periods shows the average Canadian mutual fund underperforms its benchmark index once fees are taken into consideration, leaving less money invested to grow over time. Many mutual funds consistently beat their benchmarks even after fees, but limited disclosure requirements make it difficult for average investors to find the best ones. That lack of transparency opens the door to what is called “shadow indexing”, where actively-managed portfolios bear a striking resemblance to their benchmark indices. Investors are basically paying for active management and getting a passive index fund. ETFs allow you to buy the benchmarks With index-linked ETFs, the entire market is your manager. In its purest form, passive management attempts to replicate broader indices by tracking individual holdings based on their weighting in the index and adjusting them daily as they change in value. No arbitrary decisions are made. They set it and forget it. Unlike mutual funds, holdings and their weightings in index-linked ETFs are transparent. Price changes in S&P 500 ETFs, for example, will reflect price changes in the actual S&P 500. ETFs can also provide access to a diversified array of sectors and geographic regions at a fraction of the cost. The MER on basic index-linked ETFs that track major indices could be as low as one-tenth of a per cent. The downside of index-linked ETFs While major stock market indices have always gone up over time, the market is not so good at anticipating shorter-term volatility. ETFs have no active manager to assess and steer clear of riskier holdings in an index or determine when it’s time to sell over-valued holdings and take profits. The success of ETFs has also moved providers to blur the line between passive and active management through “hybrid” or “smart” ETFs that apply arbitrary formulas. As ETFs become more elaborate, fees tend to rise.
